newsitem.title: UK: DMG sees grim outlook for Brazil EI "donkey" bond.
newsitem.headline: DMG sees grim outlook for Brazil EI "donkey" bond.

text.p: The outlook for Brazil's Eligible Interest (EI) bonds is likely to be poor amid increasing competition from new sovereign issues and a trust product launched earlier on Wednesday, Deutsche Morgan Grenfell said.
Dubbing the EI bonds a "donkey", Deutsche Morgan Grenfell said the impulse to sell EIs for other Brazilian instruments would not diminish.
"Will the urge to sell EIs relative to other Brazilian paper continue? It strikes us that it will," said Paul Luke, DMG's head of emerging market research.

Earlier on Wednesday, Bear Stearns launched a $1.28 billion multi-year deposit facility agreement (MYDFA) on behalf of the billionaire Dart family, holders of some $1.3 billion in Brazilian debt that was not restructured as Brady bonds.
The deal securitises all of Brazil's remaining loans and will be priced today to yield 110-120 basis points over EIs.
Luke said the pricing of that new MYDFA trust product would make the EIs look unattractive.

"Currently, EIs trade at 87.5 percent for a spread of 390 basis points over U.S. Treasuries. If the MYDFA product comes out at 100 basis points above EIs, the equivalent price would be 84.75 percent," he said.

"If the new product traded down to EIs, the price would be 88.5 percent of face value," he added. "Although the probable lack of liquidity will prevent such an equivalence, EIs certainly look pricy relative to the product."
Luke saw EIs also facing competition from sovereign issues.
Brazil is readying a new sovereign deal, a $750 million global likely to mature, like EIs, in 2006. The sovereign deal was expected to be priced at 375 basis points over Treasuries.

"True, such an issue has a longer average life than EIs, but it is not easy to imagine EIs trading through such an asset," he said, adding that should EIs trade down to 375 b.p. over, raising their price by 75 cents.
EIs were unlikely to be a priority in any Brazilian debt buy-back, which seems to focus on cashflow savings and cheapness, qualities more readily found in Brazil's IDU bonds.
"All in all, EIs are donkeys and anyone who holds them im preference to other Brazilian assets is, to quote Dickens, an ass," he said. --Caroline Brothers, London Newsroom +44 171 542 2734
